content.title: About
content.content: Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata) is a leafy vegetable that forms a dense, round head of tightly wrapped leaves. It is a member of the cruciferous family, along with broccoli and kale, and comes in green, red, and savoy varieties. Cabbage has a crisp texture and a mild, slightly peppery flavor and is eaten raw, cooked, or fermented.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cabbage was domesticated from wild cabbage native to the coasts of Europe.
Fermented cabbage is the basis of sauerkraut and kimchi.
Red cabbage gets its color from anthocyanins, which change color with acidity and can act as a natural pH indicator.
Cabbage has been grown for thousands of years and is a staple in many cuisines.
Cabbage keeps well for weeks, which made it an important winter vegetable.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C and vitamin K
items.content: Cabbage provides vitamin C for immune support and vitamin K for normal blood clotting.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Cabbage contributes fiber that supports normal digestion.

items.title: Contains plant compounds
items.content: Cabbage contains glucosinolates, and red cabbage contains anthocyanins, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Cabbage is low in calories and filling, making it a nutrient-dense choice.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Cabbage can cause gas or bloating in sensitive individuals, especially when raw.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables contain compounds that may affect thyroid function in very large amounts. People with thyroid conditions should consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Cabbage contains vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

items.title: Salt in fermented products
items.content: Sauerkraut and kimchi can be high in sodium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cabbage can be eaten raw in salads and coleslaw or cooked by steaming, sautéing, roasting, boiling, or braising. It can be stuffed, added to soups and stews, or fermented. Avoid overcooking, which can make it mushy and strong-smelling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole cabbage in the refrigerator crisper drawer, where it can keep for several weeks. Wrap cut cabbage tightly and use it within a few days. Wash it just before use and remove any wilted outer leaves.
